chunks: And it is reported that the Commander of the Faithful (may God's blessings be upon him) said in one of his sermons:

Had God, Majestic is His praise, intended for His prophets, when He sent them, to open for them the treasures of gold and the mines of pure ore and the plantations of gardens, and to gather the birds of the sky and the beasts of the land along with them — He would have done so. But had He done so, trials would have ceased, recompense would have been nullified, tidings (divine commandments) would have dissolved, those who merely profess belief would not have merited the rewards of those truly tested, believers would not have attained the reward of the righteous, and names (titles of honor) would not have been binding upon those who deserve them with a clear meaning.

For that reason, had God sent down a sign from the sky that caused their necks to bow in submission, had He done that, the trials would have been lifted from all people altogether. But God, Majestic is His praise, made His messengers possessors of strength in the resolve of their intentions yet appearing weak in what the eyes could observe of their outward condition — a contentment whose self-sufficiency fills the hearts and the eyes, and a poverty whose hardship fills the ears and the sight.

Had the prophets been people of invincible strength and unassailable might, and had they possessed a dominion toward which men's necks would crane and to which the belts of their mounts would be drawn tight, it would have been easier upon creation in the matter of trial and would have kept them further from arrogance, and they would have believed out of an overpowering dread upon them or an inclining desire — and so intentions would have been mixed and good deeds divided.

But God willed that the following of His messengers, the affirmation of His books, the humility before His countenance, the submission to His command, and the surrender to His obedience be matters belonging exclusively to Him, untainted by any other admixture.

And the greater the trial and the test, the more abundant the reward and the recompense. Do you not see that God, Majestic is His praise, tested the earliest of mankind from the time of Adam to the last of them in this world, with stones that neither harm nor benefit, neither see nor hear? He made them into His Sacred House which He established for people as a place of standing. Then He placed it in the most rugged terrain of the earth in stone, the least fertile of lands in soil, the narrowest of valleys in livelihood, and the harshest of places for Muslims in water — between rough mountains, soft sands, trickling springs, isolated villages, and faint traces of rain that cannot sustain camel hooves, cloven feet, or horse hooves alike.

Then He commanded Adam and his children to direct their steps toward it, and so it became a resort for the journeys they seek and a destination for resting their mounts. The fruits of hearts incline toward it from connected expanses of desert, from the islands of distant seas, and from the depths of vast ravines — until they stoop their shoulders in humility, extolling God's praises around it, walking upon their feet disheveled and dusty for His sake, having cast their head-coverings and their cloaks behind their backs and shaved their hair from their heads.

A grievous tribulation, a great trial, a severe examination, a thorough purification, and a manifest devotion — God made it a cause for His mercy, a bond and a means to His paradise, a reason for His forgiveness, and a trial for His creation through His mercy.

Had God, Blessed and Exalted, placed His Sacred House and His great rites between gardens and rivers, ease and fertile plains, with abundant trees, close-hanging fruits, dense vegetation, connected towns, dark fertile soil, green meadows, encircling rural fields, well-watered spreads, thriving crops, well-traveled roads, and plentiful orchards — the recompense would have diminished proportionate to the weakness of the trial.

Then, had the foundation it rests upon and the stones raised within it been set among green emeralds, red rubies, light and radiance — that would have eased the struggle against doubt in the chests, and would have suppressed the striving against Iblis in the hearts, and would have dispelled the wavering of uncertainty from the people. But God, Mighty and Majestic, tests His servants with varieties of hardship, and subjects them to worship through forms of striving, and tries them with kinds of difficulty — to extract arrogance from their hearts and to instill lowliness in their souls.
And He made all of this to be opened gates to His grace and lowly causes for His forgiveness and His trial,

just as He said: 'Alif Lam Meem. Do the people think they will be left to say: We believe — and not be tried? And We have certainly tried those before them, so God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars.'

key_terms.التَّذَلُّلُ: Lowliness, humility — the spiritual quality that trials cultivate
key_terms.التَّكَبُّرُ: Arrogance, pride — the spiritual disease that trials are designed to uproot
key_terms.الِاخْتِبَارُ: Testing, examination — God's deliberate testing of human beings
key_terms.الْبَلَاءُ: Trial, tribulation — the divinely ordained testing of creation
key_terms.الْبَيْتُ الْحَرَامُ: The Sacred House — the Kaaba in Mecca
key_terms.الْجَزَاءُ: Recompense, divine reward proportionate to the severity of trial

ai.seo_question: Why did God place the Kaaba in a barren and difficult location according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This is an excerpt from a sermon attributed to Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS), addressed to his companions and likely delivered in Kufa. In it, the Imam explains the profound theological wisdom underlying divine testing: if God had endowed His prophets with worldly power and wealth, or made belief compulsory through overwhelming signs, then faith would lose its moral value because intentions would be impure — mixed with fear or self-interest. True belief must be voluntary, sincere, and free from any motivation except genuine submission to God. The Imam then illustrates this principle through the example of the Kaaba: God deliberately placed His Sacred House in a harsh, barren, and difficult environment so that pilgrims who travel to it do so through hardship and sacrifice alone, ensuring that their devotion is pure. The greater the test, the greater the reward.
